title: Frontier Industries to Reshape China's Economy and Markets
summary: China’s technology transformation should reward selected frontier industry leaders in the next 12 to 18 months, reshaping corporate earnings ahead of a broad macro recovery.
body_markdown:
*Source: Morgan Stanley Research estimates*


In Morgan Stanley Research’s base case, average annual earnings growth for companies in the MSCI China Index accelerates from an estimated 6% in 2026 to an average of 11.6% annually over 2028–2030. China’s total stock-market capitalization is forecast to rise from $22.6 trillion in 2026 to $33.2 trillion by 2030, with technology, industrials and healthcare accounting for approximately 70% of the increase.


### **Why the Economic Boost Coud Be Delayed**


The benefits for China’s broader economy are unlikely to arrive immediately.


Morgan Stanley Research sees 2026 and 2027 as a transition period, where weak domestic demand and excess capacity will likely constrain overall growth, even though spending on AI computing, data centers and power grids should still benefit select companies. Job displacement and the costs of reorganizing businesses around new technologies could also offset some early productivity gains.


Starting in 2028, however, the benefits should spread as factories use capacity more efficiently and businesses deploy new technologies more broadly. AI and industrial upgrades are likely to add 0.3 percentage points to China’s annual potential economic growth from 2028 through 2030, helping support annual growth of 4.2%.


“Corporate profitability could therefore improve before household demand fully normalizes,” Wang says.


That sequencing has important implications for investors. Waiting for every major economic indicator to recover could mean overlooking companies whose earnings are already improving. At the same time, strength in technology does not mean businesses dependent on property or consumer spending will recover at the same pace.


Once the gains take hold, China’s domestic market could act as an accelerant. Its scale allows companies to reach production volumes large enough to support dedicated suppliers, purpose-built equipment and rapid experimentation. Intense competition, meanwhile, pushes companies to improve productivity and continually pressure suppliers on performance and price.


“These factors form a self-reinforcing sequence: a large domestic market enables rapid deployment, deployment generates operating feedback, feedback drives engineering improvement, improvement lowers cost, lower cost raises adoption and adoption returns as greater scale,” says Robin Xing, Morgan Stanley’s Chief China Economist.


China’s large electricity base could also help frontier industries scale rapidly with AI. Data centers account for around 2% of electricity consumption in China, compared with more than 6% in the U.S. Together with expanding power grids and battery storage, that capacity could allow AI projects to come online sooner and at lower cost, supporting broader adoption.


### **A Broadening Opportunity Set**


The earliest beneficiaries of China’s latest investment wave are likely to include semiconductor companies, technology-hardware suppliers, power-infrastructure businesses and advanced-materials producers.


From 2027–2028, opportunities could broaden into automation, robotics, machinery, batteries and manufacturers expanding overseas. AI applications, software revenues and healthcare innovation could create additional profit pools over the longer term.


“For investors, mainland-listed A shares may be preferable for their deeper exposure to these industries, while Hong Kong can serve as an important complementary market,” Wang says. “In our base case, changes in China’s global benchmark weights could imply an estimated $53 billion in additional equity allocations by 2030.”


The implications extend beyond Chinese equities. Global suppliers of industrial equipment, critical materials and power infrastructure could benefit from investment both within China and in competing supply chains elsewhere, according to Wang. At the same time, established manufacturers could face stronger competition from Chinese companies, potentially intensifying global trade tensions.


### **What Could Make the Outlook Better or Worse?**


China’s transformation could unfold faster or more slowly than Morgan Stanley Research’s base case.


In the bull case, average annual earnings growth for the MSCI China Index could reach 14%, as stronger domestic demand reinforces productivity gains from AI and industrial upgrading.


“This scenario requires policymakers to act faster to stabilize housing, strengthen the social safety net and encourage consumption,” Xing says. “This allows companies to sell more of what they can produce and retain more of their efficiency gains as profits.”


In the bear case, average annual earnings growth for the MSCI China Index is limited to 6%, if weak demand, less disciplined investment and restricted access to overseas markets and technology prevent technological progress from translating into stronger profits and a broader economic recovery.


Another risk is “smart overcapacity.” Excessive investment could leave too many companies producing similar technologies, intensifying competition and eroding the profits that greater productivity would otherwise generate.
